Key findings from the 520-page final report of the US House of Representatives Special Subcommittee on the COVID-19 pandemic

This is one of the most detailed official documents that directly refutes or significantly weakens many of the claims that dominated in the years 2020-2022.

Here are the strongest and most devastating points against the propaganda at that time:

1. Virus Origins
COVID-19 most likely came from a lab in Wuhan (a lab incident related to gain-of-function research).
Five key arguments in favor of the lab theory: biological features of the virus rarely found in nature; all early cases point to a single introduction into the population; dangerous research was conducted at the Wuhan Institute of Virology with insufficient biosafety levels; institute staff had COVID-like illness in fall 2019; no convincing evidence of a natural origin has been found over the years.

2. Social Distancing
The "6 feet" rule (approximately 2 meters) was not based on scientific data.
Anthony Fauci directly stated in closed testimony that it "sort of just appeared”.

3. Masks
There was no convincing evidence that masks effectively protect the population from COVID-19.
Authorities changed positions multiple times without providing data, which greatly undermined trust.

4. Lockdowns
Extended lockdowns caused immeasurable harm to the economy, physical and mental health of people, especially the youth - a group with the lowest risk of severe disease.
Closing schools was not justified by science. Children rarely spread the virus and rarely became severely ill, but they suffered historic losses in education, psychological damage, and deteriorating physical health (including a sharp rise in suicide attempts among girls aged 12-17).

5. Vaccines and Mandates
Vaccines did not stop the transmission of the virus (contrary to initial claims).
Mandates lacked sufficient scientific support, ignored natural immunity, caused harm, and seriously limited personal freedoms.
Promises that "get vaccinated – and protect others" turned out to be false.

6. Overall government interventions conclusion
The report directly states that many key measures (distancing, masks, prolonged lockdowns, school closures, and mandates) either lacked solid scientific basis or did more harm than good. Authorities and some of the scientific community actively suppressed alternative viewpoints (including the lab origin theory) and used censorship.

These findings are particularly strong because they are made not by bloggers, but by an official subcommittee of the US Congress after a two-year investigation with access to documents, testimonies, and internal communications. That is why they remain one of the most serious blows to the 2020-2022 narrative to this day.

📌 Bridges: How Assets Move Between Blockchains

Main Points
⏺ Bridges move tokens across chains by locking on one side and issuing an equivalent on the other
⏺ They unlock liquidity and DeFi flows, but bridges are among the most attacked surfaces in crypto
⏺ This post explains how bridges work — and where security usually breaks

1️⃣ Core Mechanic — assets get locked on Chain A, and an equivalent is minted/released on Chain B via messaging.
2️⃣ Bridge Designs — some are trusted, some are trust-minimized, but implementation details matter everywhere.
3️⃣ Risk Hotspots — smart contract bugs, compromised relayers/validators, broken message verification.
4️⃣ User Impact — many of crypto’s biggest losses happen on bridges: one failure can wipe out liquidity.
5️⃣ Risk Control — stick to battle-tested bridges, look for audits/history, split transfers, avoid fresh bridges with no track record.

Final Thoughts

Bridges create freedom of movement — but they’re a thin layer of trust. If the bridge breaks, access breaks.

🟠 Nine Major Firms Launch $15M Bitcoin Security Consortium

BlackRock, Coinbase, Strategy, Fidelity Digital Assets, Anchorage Digital, ARK Invest, Block, Blockstream, and Galaxy have formed the Bitcoin Security Consortium, pledging $15 million over three years to fund open-source developers and advance quantum-resistant security research for the Bitcoin network.

Announced July 23, the consortium will direct funding independently, with members taking no role in Bitcoin governance or protocol decisions. Research priorities include post-quantum cryptography and long-term network resilience against potential future quantum-computing threats.

The initiative reflects growing institutional concern over quantum computing's long-term risk to Bitcoin's cryptographic foundations, with participants spanning Wall Street asset managers, crypto exchanges, and infrastructure providers.

Is an All-Out War in the Middle East Put On Hold? 

😀😀😀😀 😀😀😀

Over the weekend, Trump rejected a return to full-scale war. But as he tries to find a way out of a conflict he started, Iran has proved a stubborn enemy.

On Tuesday evening, Iran fired multiple missiles on American bases in Jordan. The U.S. military intercepted the missiles with apparent ease, but the incident has drawn Trump once again back into fighting.

The United States struck back in a “powerful response” against Iran on Wednesday evening, U.S. Central Command said on social media. “We’re going to be hitting them very hard, because it’s our turn to hit them,” Trump told reporters earlier in the day.

The Iranian and U.S. moves come as the war has widened quickly, with Saudi Arabia joining U.S. forces in striking Iranian proxies in Iraq, an American tanker in Egypt set ablaze from an apparent drone strike and tensions rising between Ukraine and Iran.

The war, which Trump has been trying to bring to a diplomatic conclusion since April, is now threatening to grow bigger at the very moment the United States wants to move past it.

“When Trump started the war, he thought he could control it,” said Vali Nasr, a professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies. “The Iranian response is to extend the battlefield much, much wider, so the United States has to defend a broader battlefield.”

Experts said that at this stage in the war, which the United States launched with Israel five months ago, Iran wants to demonstrate the military adage that the enemy always gets a vote.

Iran wanted to demonstrate that they are not going to sit back and wait for the U.S. or Israel to strike at a time of their preference,” said Jason Campbell of the Middle East Institute. “They are trying to seize the initiative, or at the very least keep the U.S. and Israel on their back foot.”

U.S. military commanders prepared a plan for Mr. Trump that would have started another days-long bombing campaign. U.S. forces had moved air assets to Israel in preparation for those attacks, and those planes remain in place should Trump change his mind in the face of the Iranian action.

In the deliberations over that plan, Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, cautioned privately that resuming major combat operations against Iran was doable but would dangerously deplete interceptors available to the military’s Central Command, according to two people briefed on the discussions.

Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of Central Command, said that if Trump did not resume major combat operations, the United States should stop the bombing campaign around the Strait of Hormuz because it has reached the limit of its effectiveness, the two officials said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters.
